title: The Mool Mantar, sounded
hookLine: Ik Onkar, Satnam, Karta Purakh, Nirbhau, Nirvair, Akal Murat, Ajuni, Saibhang, Gur Prasad

cards: Every community has a line people know by heart, words that come out without thinking, at a wedding, a funeral, a bedside. Sikhs have one that comes before everything else. It opens the Guru Granth Sahib.
It opens Japji. A short form of it stands at the head of hymns all through the scripture. It's the Mool Mantar, the root verse.
Today, no explaining. Just how it sounds.

teach.b: Mool means root. Mantar is a verse to be repeated. The root verse.
Here it is, slowly, in its pieces. Ik Onkar. Ik, like ick; Onkar, ong-KAAR.
Sat Naam. Sat, rhyming with but; naam, like calm with an n. Kartaa Purakh.
KAR-taa, PUR-akh. Nirbhau. nir-BHOW, like now, with a breath on the b. Nirvair. nir-VAIR, like air.
Akaal Moorat. a-KAAL, MOO-rat. Ajoonee. a-JOO-nee. Saibhang. say-BHUNG.
Gur Prasaad. gur pra-SAAD. That's the whole thing: fourteen short words, the way they're spaced here. Said slowly, it takes less than half a minute.

You met some of their meanings back on days ten and eleven, and you'll keep meeting them all through Japji: one; truth is the name; the maker; without fear; without hate; beyond time; unborn; self-existent; known by the Guru's grace.
It moves in short beats, two and three syllables at a time, easy to breathe with.
Its first sound is a number: ik, one. Its middle is a run of nirs and a's, nirbhau, nirvair, akaal, ajoonee, each saying what the One is not: not afraid, not hating, not bound by time, not born.
And the last two words, gur prasaad, turn the whole verse into a gift: not something you figure out, but something given.
Sikhs differ a little on where the Mool Mantar ends. Some end it at gur prasaad. Others carry on through the next lines, to Naanak hosee bhee sach.
Either way, every word of it is said each morning at the start of Japji.

how: Sikhs recite the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji each morning and at many other moments; a short form, Ik Onkar Satgur Prasad, stands at the head of hymns throughout the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: the root verse that opens the Guru Granth Sahib
a secret phrase a teacher whispers to a student
a prayer for good weather before the harvest

games.q: match the sound to its sense.

s: the Mool Mantar is a long passage
it's fourteen short words, as we spaced them, and takes less than half a minute to say slowly.
its very first sound is a number
every Sikh ends it at exactly the same word
some end at gur prasaad; others carry on to Naanak hosee bhee sach.

games.q: the Mool Mantar is a short verse. what is its very first sound?
games.why: ik, one. the whole Guru Granth Sahib begins with a number.

practice: Sit up, breathe in, and say it slowly, out loud if you can, in a whisper if you can't, with a breath between each piece: Ik Onkar, Sat Naam, Kartaa Purakh, Nirbhau, Nirvair, Akaal Moorat, Ajoonee, Saibhang, Gur Prasaad.
Then say it once more, a little smoother, without worrying about every vowel; say what you heard. If you pray, it's already a prayer; if you're learning, it's a sound worth knowing by heart.
